changes.before: Earth becomes one moving planet among others. This model offers new explanations for familiar observations rather than discarding those observations.
changes.after: In Copernicus's model, Earth and the other planets orbit the Sun. Earth is a moving planet, not the stationary centre of the heavens.

changes.before: The optical effect is surprising, but its setup can be examined and repeated. Other people can check whether the same arrangement produces the same result.
changes.after: Light passing through a small opening forms an upside-down image inside a dark box. Other people can inspect and repeat the setup to check whether it produces the same image.

changes.before: Newton joins terrestrial and celestial motion in a common system using absolute space and time. Later theories must explain both its successes and its limits.
changes.after: Newton describes motion on Earth and in the sky in one system. He assumes space exists independently of the objects in it, and time passes alike everywhere. Later theories must explain both the system's successes and its limits.

changes.before: Observations of the Moon, compared with prepared tables, supply a reference time. This relies on both earlier records and present observations.
changes.after: The Moon changes position against the stars as time passes. A navigator can compare its measured position with prepared tables to find the time at a known place.

changes.before: The Moon can provide the time comparison needed for longitude. This is a genuine alternative to a sea clock, with different demands on weather and observation.
changes.after: A navigator compares the Moon’s measured position with prepared tables to find the time at a known place. Comparing that time with local time gives the east–west position. This is an alternative to carrying a sea clock, but needs a clear view of the sky.

changes.before: The layers can be placed in order from earlier to later. This establishes a sequence without yet giving ages in years.
changes.after: Rock layers can be placed in order from earlier to later. This establishes a sequence without yet giving ages in years.

changes.before: Lamarck treats species as changing through use, disuse and inherited acquired changes. His proposed explanation differs from later accounts based on natural selection.
changes.after: Lamarck argues that use and disuse change an organism's body, and those changes can pass to its offspring. This differs from natural selection, which acts on inherited differences already present.

changes.before: The compass response shows that electricity can have a magnetic effect. Forces need not work through a visible mechanical push.
changes.after: An electric current makes a nearby compass needle turn. This shows that electricity can have a magnetic effect without a visible mechanical push.

changes.before: No preferred inertial frame or universal distant present
changes.after: No universal time for distant events

changes.before: Observers moving steadily relative to one another use the same physical laws but need not agree on distant simultaneity. Newton's mechanics remains a useful approximation in everyday conditions.
changes.after: Observers moving steadily past one another use the same physical laws and measure the same speed of light. They can still disagree about whether far-apart events happened at the same time. Newton's mechanics remains a useful approximation at everyday speeds.

changes.before: The patterns support movement, but the proposed driving forces remain inadequate. Evidence for a history can be stronger than its current explanation of how it happened.
changes.after: Matching fossils and rocks suggest that continents once joined have moved apart, but Wegener did not have a convincing account of the force moving them. Evidence that they moved can be stronger than the current explanation of how.

changes.before: New ocean floor forms at ridges and moves away on both sides. This process explains the paired magnetic patterns.
changes.after: New ocean floor forms at ridges and spreads out on both sides. As its rock cools, it records Earth's magnetic direction. Matching bands on opposite sides of a ridge show that the floor has moved outward.

changes.before: More greenhouse gas changes how heat escapes to space. The warming mechanism depends on the gas's interaction with infrared radiation.
changes.after: Earth's surface gives off heat as infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit some of it, reducing the heat escaping directly to space. The surface and lower atmosphere warm until outgoing heat again balances incoming sunlight.

changes.before: Roman law divides people by legal status in ways different from Greek political participation. Comparing the two systems does not make them identical.
changes.after: Roman law distinguishes freeborn, freed and enslaved people. Those legal statuses give people different rights and are not the same as citizenship or participation in government in a Greek city.

changes.before: Venus is observed in both crescent and nearly full phases. That range conflicts with the standard Ptolemaic arrangement of Venus. It rules out that arrangement, not every model in which Earth stays still.
changes.after: Ptolemy's standard model keeps Venus on Earth's side of the Sun, so it cannot show nearly full phases. Observing those phases rules out that arrangement, but not every model in which Earth stays still.

changes.before: Lead in blank laboratory tests reveals contamination that interferes with dating ancient material. Comparing older and modern environments turns that measurement problem into evidence of industrial lead pollution.
changes.after: Lead appears even in laboratory tests without an ancient sample, revealing contamination that interferes with dating. Comparing older and modern environments turns that measurement problem into evidence of industrial lead pollution.

changes.after: Lamarck explains species change through bodily changes acquired during life and passed to offspring. Darwin and Wallace's account of natural selection instead concerns inherited differences that affect survival and reproduction. They agree that species change, but differ about how.

changes.before: The flashes are simultaneous in the platform frame. In the train frame, equal paths and the same light speed mean their different arrival times imply different emission times. The disagreement concerns simultaneity after accounting for travel time, not just a delayed signal.
changes.after: Two flashes happen at a moving train's ends at the same time according to platform clocks, but their light reaches a passenger at the train's midpoint at different times. For the passenger, light travels equal distances from the two ends at the same speed. The passenger therefore concludes that the flashes happened at different times.

changes.before: Flashes simultaneous by platform clocks reach the moving train midpoint at different times. This establishes different arrival times. To infer emission times in the train frame, the equal distances and speed of light there must also be considered.

A passenger at the moving train's midpoint travels toward one flash and away from the other, so their light reaches the passenger at different times. These arrival times alone do not yet show when the flashes happened for the passenger.

changes.before: Travel with a kitchen caravan from a roadside breakfast through an orchard, a rainy market and the railway kitchens. Keep cooking in each kitchen while its people need you, then take your useful preparations onward. The journey ends by sending a real supper aboard the departing train. This fictional collection is not a chronology of invention; time, proportions and safe handling are compressed, not taught. A staffed pantry cart and managed cold storage keep saved ingredients and preparations under the cooks’ care between stops; some of the breakfast juice is reserved for the journey.

changes.before: Hands and a book show that the rite uses physical objects. They do not establish whether its community believed in one good creator or opposed sources. The Lyon ritual and the Book of Two Principles must not be merged into one universal Cathar doctrine.
changes.after: In the Lyon ritual, ministers lay hands and a Gospel book on a believer while promising forgiveness and God’s Spirit. Using physical objects does not tell us whether this community believed in one good creator or opposed sources of good and evil. The Book of Two Principles argues for opposed sources; the ritual does not state that account.

changes.before: Aquinas: “grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it” — gloss: God’s help develops human powers rather than erasing them
changes.after: Aquinas: “grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it”

changes.before: For Aquinas, baptism washes the body while God works through the rite to give inward grace. The water is God's instrument, not a second god. This depends on his further belief that God appointed baptism; ordinary water is not automatically a sacrament.
changes.after: For Aquinas, baptism washes the body while God works through the water to give grace: a new life within the soul. The water is a tool, not a second god. This depends on his belief that God chose baptism to give that gift.

changes.before: Tasting the bread cannot prove the change Aquinas describes, because he says its taste remains. His account rests on faith in divine authority, not on a hidden change detected by the senses.
changes.after: Aquinas says the bread becomes Christ’s body while its taste remains. Tasting it therefore cannot prove the change he claims. His account rests on faith in divine authority, not a change detected by the senses.

changes.before: Luther gives household necessities and help for poor neighbours priority over buying an indulgence. With one coin and no supper, the household should buy food first.
changes.after: Luther says a household with one coin and no supper should buy food before an indulgence letter—a grant of relief from penalties for sins already forgiven. Feeding the family and helping poor neighbours come first.

changes.before: A person can serve God without controlling God's gifts. Comparing Luther's limits on church authority with Aquinas's dependent instrument clarifies that distinction without making their doctrines identical.
changes.after: Luther says church ministers can announce God’s forgiveness but cannot make God forgive for money. Aquinas says baptism’s water acts through God’s power, not its own. Both distinguish serving God from independently controlling God’s gifts, although they address different practices.

changes.before:
God’s working through baptism shows a possible role for created means; water is not a person being asked for prayer. That example does not authorize addressing departed saints.

Calvin affirms Christ’s unique, continuing work of bringing people before God. He says asking departed saints lacks biblical permission and obscures that work. He is objecting to the practice, not doubting Christ’s role.
changes.after: Aquinas says God can work through baptism’s water. But water is not a person being asked to pray, so this example does not decide whether people should address saints who have died. Calvin rejects those requests: he says they lack biblical permission and obscure Christ’s unique work of bringing people before God.
